newsitem.title: USA: US yield curve shows 3.7 pct GDP growth to Q2 '98.
newsitem.headline: US yield curve shows 3.7 pct GDP growth to Q2 '98.

text.p: The steep U.S. Treasury yield curve is predicting the U.S. Gross Domestic Product will grow at an average of 3.7 percent from the second quarter of 1997 through the first quarter of 1998, an economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland said on Monday.
"The yield curve currently predicts growth of about 3.7 percent over the next four quarters," Cleveland Fed economist Joseph Haubrich told Reuters.
Haubrich stressed that his forecast was not aimed at predicting any Fed policy decisions during that period.
The spread between the three-month bill and the 10-year Treasury note currently stands at 142 basis points, steeper than the average 120 basis points recorded since the early 1960s.
The Cleveland Fed's work is consistent with a 1996 research paper authored by New York Fed director of research Frederic Mishkin and senior vice president Arturo Estrella.
That study dealt with the yield curve's ability to predict changes in business cycles and was based on the same spread as the one used by Haubrich and over a similar period.
The Mishkin-Estrella study put the odds of a recession over the next four quarters at less than 5.0 percent.

"The yield curve is saying the market feels economic growth will be relatively strong," said Haubrich, whose model last September predicted 3.4-percent average GDP growth for the period mid-1996 to mid-1997.
GDP grew by 2.1 percent in the third quarter of 1996, 3.8 percent in the fourth quarter and 5.6 percent in the first quarter of 1997, according to an initial estimate.
"The yield curve had small ups and downs but it has been the same essentially," Haubrich said, noting the yield curve's solid track record as a predictor of economic performance.
Haubrich acknowledged the correlation between the yield curve and the economy has been less tight between the mid-1980s and the mid-1990s, possibly due to changes in the economy.
"But it is returning to a good correlation, although the correlation seems somewhat different than it was in the past," Haubrich noted.

Asked whether the trend of smaller U.S. budget deficits may be a factor helping to restore a tight relationship between the yield curve and the economy, Haubrich said "My feeling is this would not have a big influence."
Haubrich added the yield curve would pick up such fiscal changes only to the extent that it readily translates into changes in economic growth.

"If you change fiscal policy, this is going to have a real effect on the economy," a change the yield curve would reflect because it "is picking up on what affects the economy is going on in the policy."
"It's not showing signs of the end of the recovery. It's consistent with other things we know."
